title: Pork guisantes
intro: Pork simmered in a light tomato sauce with plenty of sweet green peas and red bell pepper. It is simpler than afritada, with no potatoes or carrots, and quick to put together on a weeknight.

items.name: pork shoulder (kasim)
items.note: cut into thin strips or 1-inch cubes

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat and sauté the garlic, onion and tomatoes until the tomatoes soften.
Add the pork and cook, stirring, until it changes color.
Add the fish sauce and cook for a minute, then pour in the tomato sauce and water. Bring to a boil.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the bell pepper and peas and simmer, uncovered, until the sauce thickens.
Season with salt and pepper and serve with rice.

tips: Frozen peas taste sweeter than canned and keep their color. Add them right at the end so they do not turn gray.

title: Pork giniling
intro: Ground pork sautéed with tomato sauce, diced potatoes, carrots, peas and raisins until saucy and a little sweet. It cooks in about half an hour, keeps well, and is a common baon for school and work.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and sauté the onion and garlic until soft.
Add the ground pork and cook, breaking it up, until it is no longer pink and starts to brown.
Add the soy sauce and fish sauce and cook for a minute.
Stir in the tomato sauce, water, potatoes and carrots. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer until the potatoes are tender.
Add the peas, raisins and sugar and simmer, uncovered, until the sauce thickens.
Season with salt and pepper and serve with rice.

tips: Dice the potatoes and carrots small so they cook through in the same time as the meat. Leftovers make a good filling for tortang giniling or pandesal.

title: Beef giniling
intro: Ground beef cooked down in tomato sauce with diced potatoes and red and green bell peppers. It is savory rather than sweet, quick to make, and good over rice or tucked into pandesal.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and fry the potatoes until lightly golden. Set aside.
Sauté the onion and garlic in the same pan until soft.
Add the ground beef and cook, breaking it up, until browned and any liquid has cooked off.
Stir in the tomato paste for a minute, then add the tomato sauce, water and soy sauce. Return the potatoes and simmer, covered, until tender.
Add the bell peppers and sugar and simmer, uncovered, until the sauce is thick.
Season with salt and pepper and serve.

tips: Ground beef releases more liquid than pork. Let it cook off completely before adding the tomato paste so the beef browns instead of steaming.

title: Beef picadillo
intro: Ground beef and diced potatoes simmered in a light, brothy tomato soup seasoned with fish sauce. It is the soupier cousin of giniling, ladled over rice on rainy days.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat and sauté the garlic, onion and tomatoes until the tomatoes break down.
Add the ground beef and cook, breaking it up, until no longer pink.
Add the fish sauce and cook for a minute, then pour in the water and bring to a boil. Skim off any scum.
Add the potatoes and simmer until tender.
Season with pepper and more fish sauce if needed. Stir in the green onions and serve hot.

tips: For a heartier bowl, add a handful of misua noodles in the last 2 minutes.

title: Giniling with quail eggs
intro: Ground pork in a saucy tomato base with potatoes, carrots, bell pepper and whole quail eggs that soak up the sauce. It stretches half a kilo of giniling into a meal for four.

steps.text: Put the quail eggs in a small pot of cold water, bring to a boil and boil.
Cool the eggs in cold water, then peel.
Heat the oil in a pan and sauté the onion and garlic until soft. Add the ground pork and cook until browned. Add the fish sauce.
Stir in the tomato sauce, water, potatoes and carrots. Cover and simmer until the vegetables are tender.
Add the quail eggs, bell pepper and sugar and simmer, uncovered, so the eggs take on the sauce.
Season with salt and pepper and serve.

tips: Peel quail eggs under running water, starting from the wide end where the air pocket is. Canned quail eggs work too; just drain and rinse them.

title: Pork and beans
intro: Canned pork and beans stretched into a full ulam with browned pork belly, tomato sauce and onions. It is sweet, savory and quick, and goes with plain rice.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat and cook the pork belly, stirring now and then, until browned and much of the fat has rendered. Pour off all but 1 tbsp fat.
Add the onion and garlic and cook until soft. Add the fish sauce.
Pour in the tomato sauce and water. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the pork and beans, hotdogs and brown sugar and simmer until the sauce thickens.
Season with salt and pepper and serve with rice.

tips: Taste before adding the sugar; some brands of pork and beans are already quite sweet.

title: Filipino beef stew
intro: Chunks of beef simmered in a dark, savory gravy of broth, soy sauce and a little tomato paste, with potatoes, carrots and celery. It is thicker and less tomatoey than kaldereta or mechado, and made for spooning over rice.

steps.text: Season the beef with salt and pepper and toss it with the flour.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the beef well in batches. Set aside.
Sauté the onion and garlic in the same pot until soft. Stir in the tomato paste and cook for a minute.
Return the beef and add the broth, soy sauce, Worcestershire sauce, bay leaves and sugar. Scrape up the browned bits and bring to a boil.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the beef is tender.
Add the potatoes, carrots and celery and simmer, uncovered, until tender and the gravy has thickened.
Taste for salt and pepper, remove the bay leaves and serve.

tips: If the gravy is still thin at the end, mash a few potato cubes against the side of the pot and stir them in.

title: Asadong baboy
intro: Pork braised with soy sauce, calamansi and plenty of fresh tomatoes until the sauce is thick, sweet and tangy, served topped with fried potatoes. This is the tomato-braised home version, not the red Chinese-style roast pork that shares the name.

steps.text: Toss the pork with the soy sauce, calamansi juice and pepper and marinate.
Heat the oil in a heavy pan over medium heat and fry the potato wedges until golden and cooked through. Set aside.
Lift the pork from the marinade, keeping the marinade, and brown it in the same oil.
Add the onion, garlic and tomatoes and cook until the tomatoes break down into a chunky sauce.
Add the reserved marinade, tomato paste, water, bay leaves and brown sugar. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer until the pork is tender.
Uncover and simmer until the sauce is thick and clings to the pork.
Taste for salt, then serve topped with the fried potatoes.

tips: Ripe, soft tomatoes give the sauce its body. If yours are pale or firm, add another tablespoon of tomato paste.

title: Chicken sarsiado
intro: Fried chicken simmered in a thick sauce of sautéed tomatoes and onions, with beaten egg swirled in at the end. It is mild, savory and saucy, and a good use for leftover fried chicken too.

steps.text: Season the chicken with the salt and some pepper. Heat the oil in a wide pan and fry the chicken over medium heat, turning, until golden and cooked through. Set aside.
Pour off all but 2 tbsp of the oil. Sauté the garlic, onion and tomatoes until the tomatoes are soft and mushy.
Add the tomato sauce, water and fish sauce and simmer until slightly thickened.
Return the chicken and simmer, turning the pieces in the sauce.
Pour the beaten eggs over the sauce in a thin stream. Let them set for a moment, then stir gently so they form soft ribbons.
Season with pepper, scatter the green onions on top and serve.

tips: Do not stir the eggs right away; letting them set first gives soft strands instead of a cloudy sauce.

title: Pork sarsiado
intro: Fried pork chops simmered in a tomato and onion sauce with beaten egg stirred through. It works just as well with leftover lechon kawali.

steps.text: Season the pork chops with the salt and some pepper. Fry them in the oil over medium heat until golden and cooked through, 5 to 6 minutes a side. Set aside.
Pour off all but 2 tbsp of the oil. Sauté the garlic, onion and tomatoes until the tomatoes are soft and mushy.
Add the tomato sauce, water and fish sauce and simmer until slightly thickened.
Return the pork chops and simmer, turning them once.
Pour in the beaten eggs in a thin stream. Let them set for a moment, then stir gently.
Season with pepper, top with the green onions and serve.

tips: Snip the fat along the edge of each chop in two or three places before frying so the chops stay flat.

title: Ginisang sardinas
intro: Canned sardines in tomato sauce sautéed with garlic, onion and fresh tomatoes, then simmered briefly with a long green chili. It is a cheap, fast ulam that tastes much better than sardines straight from the can.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and sauté the garlic until fragrant, then add the onion and tomatoes and cook until soft.
Add the sardines with their sauce and break them gently into large chunks.
Pour in the water, add the chili and simmer.
Season with pepper, top with the green onion and serve with rice.

tips: For a soupier version, add another cup of water and a handful of misua noodles at the end.

title: Bacalao
intro: Salted cod flaked into a tomato and olive oil stew with potatoes, bell peppers, chickpeas and olives. It is salty and rich, and often cooked for meatless days during Holy Week.

steps.text: Drain the soaked cod, put it in a pot of fresh water and bring to a simmer.
Drain, then flake the cod into large pieces, removing the skin and bones.
Heat the olive oil in a wide pot over medium heat and fry the potatoes until golden and almost tender. Set aside.
In the same oil, sauté the onion and garlic until soft, then add the tomatoes and cook until they break down.
Add the tomato sauce, water and bay leaf and simmer until slightly thickened.
Add the cod, potatoes, bell peppers, chickpeas and olives and simmer gently until the potatoes are tender.
Taste before seasoning; it usually needs only pepper. Serve with rice.

tips: Soak the cod in the fridge for 24 hours, changing the water three or four times. Taste a flake before cooking: if it is still very salty, soak it a few hours longer.

title: Lechon kaldereta
intro: Leftover lechon chopped and simmered in a spicy kaldereta sauce with liver spread, potatoes and bell peppers. The crackling softens into the sauce, and the roast pork flavor carries through the whole pot.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat and sauté the onion and garlic until soft.
Add the tomato sauce, water, bay leaves, potatoes and carrots. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer until the vegetables are almost tender.
Add the lechon and simmer so it softens and flavors the sauce.
Stir in the liver spread and chilies and simmer until the sauce thickens.
Add the bell peppers and cook until just tender.
Taste before seasoning, since lechon is often salty, then serve.

tips: Use any leftover lechon sauce in place of some of the water for a sweeter, deeper sauce.

title: Pork hamonado
intro: Pork braised in pineapple juice, soy sauce and brown sugar until the sauce reduces to a sweet, glossy glaze with chunks of pineapple. It is sweet and savory, with a light tang from the fruit.

steps.text: Combine the pork, pineapple juice and soy sauce and marinate.
Lift the pork out and keep the marinade. Pat the pork dry and brown it in the oil over medium-high heat.
Add the garlic and onion and cook until fragrant.
Pour in the marinade and water, add the brown sugar, bay leaves and pepper and bring to a boil.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the pineapple chunks and simmer, uncovered, until the sauce is thick and glossy.
Taste for salt and serve with rice.

tips: For deeper flavor, marinate the pork overnight in the fridge. Watch the pot near the end: the sugary sauce can scorch once it thickens.

title: Beef estofado
intro: Beef chuck braised slowly in soy sauce, vinegar and brown sugar, finished with carrots and fried saba bananas. The sauce is dark, sweet and tangy, and the long braise makes the beef very tender.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat and fry the saba until golden on both sides. Set aside.
Brown the beef in the same oil in batches, then add the garlic and onion and cook until fragrant.
Add the soy sauce, water, brown sugar, bay leaves and peppercorns and bring to a boil.
Pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the beef is tender, adding water if the pot gets dry.
Add the carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender and the sauce has reduced.
Add the saba and simmer until the sauce is glossy. Taste and adjust with sugar or soy sauce.

tips: Beef needs more liquid than pork for the long braise. If the sauce reduces too early, add hot water half a cup at a time.

title: Pork picadillo
intro: Ground pork, diced potatoes and carrots simmered in a light tomato broth seasoned with fish sauce. It is soupy and mild, a cheap and comforting ulam ladled over rice.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat and sauté the garlic, onion and tomatoes until the tomatoes break down.
Add the ground pork and cook, breaking it up, until it is no longer pink and some fat has rendered.
Add the fish sauce and cook for a minute, then pour in the water and bring to a boil. Skim off any scum.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer until tender.
Season with pepper and more fish sauce if needed. Stir in the green onions and serve hot.

tips: Mash a few of the potato cubes against the side of the pot at the end for a slightly thicker broth.

title: Chicken guisantes
intro: Strips of chicken simmered in a light tomato sauce with lots of green peas, carrots and red bell pepper. It is mild, a little sweet from the peas, and quick enough for a weeknight.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and sauté the garlic, onion and tomatoes until the tomatoes soften.
Add the chicken and cook, stirring, until it turns opaque. Add the fish sauce.
Pour in the tomato sauce and water and add the carrots. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer until the chicken and carrots are tender.
Add the bell pepper and peas and simmer, uncovered, until the sauce thickens.
Season with salt and pepper and serve with rice.

tips: Thigh meat stays tender in the sauce. If using breast, cut the covered simmer to 10 minutes.

title: Bola-bola in tomato sauce
intro: Pork meatballs browned and then simmered in a tomato sauce with bell pepper and green peas. They are tender and savory, and the sauce is mild and slightly sweet.

steps.text: Mix the ground pork, egg, breadcrumbs, minced onion, carrot, salt and pepper with your hands until just combined. Shape into about 20 balls.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat and brown the meatballs on all sides in batches. They do not need to be cooked through. Set aside.
Pour off all but 1 tbsp oil. Sauté the garlic, chopped onion and tomatoes until soft.
Add the tomato sauce, water, fish sauce and sugar and bring to a simmer. Return the meatballs, cover and simmer until cooked through.
Add the bell pepper and peas and simmer, uncovered, until the sauce thickens.
Taste for seasoning and serve with rice.

tips: Wet your hands while shaping so the mixture does not stick. Fry one small test meatball first to check the seasoning.

title: Pork ribs kaldereta
intro: Pork spareribs braised until tender in a spicy tomato sauce thickened with peanut butter, with potatoes, carrots and bell peppers. The bones enrich the sauce and the peanut butter makes it nutty and creamy.

steps.text: Season the ribs with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the ribs on all sides in batches. Set aside.
Pour off all but 2 tbsp of the fat and sauté the onion and garlic until soft.
Return the ribs with the tomato sauce, water and bay leaves. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer until the meat is tender and starts to pull from the bone.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender.
Whisk the peanut butter with a ladle of the sauce until smooth and stir it into the pot with the chilies. Simmer, stirring from the bottom, until thick.
Add the bell peppers and cook until they soften slightly.
Season with fish sauce, salt and pepper and serve.

tips: Ask for meaty spareribs rather than baby back ribs, which have less meat and dry out in the long simmer.

title: Pork ribs afritada
intro: Pork spareribs simmered in tomato sauce until the meat pulls from the bone, with potatoes, carrots, bell peppers and peas. The bones give the mild afritada sauce more body than boneless pork.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the ribs on all sides in batches. Pour off all but 2 tbsp of the fat.
Sauté the onion, garlic and tomatoes in the pot until the tomatoes soften.
Return the ribs, add the fish sauce and cook for a minute, then add the tomato sauce, water and bay leaves. Bring to a boil and skim.
Cover, lower the heat and simmer until the meat is tender and starts to pull from the bone.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender and the sauce has thickened.
Add the bell peppers and peas and cook until the peppers are just tender.
Season with salt and pepper and serve with rice.

tips: Simmering the ribs for 10 minutes in plain water first and draining them gives a cleaner-tasting sauce.

title: Pata kaldereta
intro: Pork hock boiled until soft and sticky, then simmered in a spicy kaldereta sauce with liver spread, cheese, potatoes and bell peppers. The gelatin from the skin makes the sauce rich and glossy.

steps.text: Put the pata, water, quartered onion and peppercorns in a large pot. Bring to a boil and skim, then cover and simmer until the skin is soft.
Lift out the pata and keep 2 cups of the broth.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot and sauté the chopped onion and garlic until soft.
Add the pata, tomato sauce, reserved broth and bay leaves. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer until the meat is very tender.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender.
Stir in the liver spread and chilies, then the bell peppers and cheese. Simmer until the cheese melts and the sauce is thick.
Season with fish sauce, salt and pepper and serve.

tips: A pressure cooker gets the pata soft in about 35 minutes. Ask the butcher to cut it into rings; it takes a heavy cleaver.

title: Pork chop afritada
intro: Pan-fried pork chops simmered whole in afritada sauce with potatoes, carrots and bell peppers. Browning the chops first gives the tomato sauce a deeper, meatier flavor, and each person gets a whole chop.

steps.text: Snip the fat along the edge of each chop in two or three places so they stay flat. Season with the salt and some pepper.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium heat and fry the potatoes and carrots until lightly browned. Set aside.
Brown the pork chops in the same oil, about 3 minutes a side. Set aside.
Sauté the onion and garlic until soft, add the fish sauce, then pour in the tomato sauce and water and add the bay leaf.
Return the chops, cover and simmer until tender, turning them once.
Add the potatoes and carrots and simmer, uncovered, until tender and the sauce has thickened.
Add the bell pepper and peas, cook for a few minutes more and serve.

tips: Thin chops toughen if they simmer too long. Use chops at least 1/2 inch thick, or shorten the covered simmer to 10 minutes.
